claims.text: High-pressure torsion combined with spark plasma sintering of mechanically alloyed powders will improve the thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr.
The initial HfNbTaTiZr material has varying oxygen content.
HfNbTaTiZr can be processed by spark plasma sintering of mechanically alloyed powders.
High-pressure torsion can be applied to spark-plasma-sintered HfNbTaTiZr samples.
The relevant HfNbTaTiZr processing pressure extends up to 50 GPa.
The applicable oxygen-content range is 0–1 wt.%.
High-pressure torsion refines the HfNbTaTiZr microstructure and reduces its grain size.
High-pressure torsion increases the dislocation density of HfNbTaTiZr.
The intervention changes chemical short-range order in HfNbTaTiZr.
Spark plasma sintering of mechanically alloyed powders optimizes the oxygen content of HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen content affects both lattice and electronic contributions to thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr.
Thermal conductivity contains distinct electronic and lattice contributions.
Microstructural refinement will reduce the lattice thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr.
The intervention will enhance total thermal conductivity at high temperature.
The exact relationship among microstructural refinement, oxygen content, and thermal conductivity is not fully understood.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome attributes enhanced total thermal conductivity to reduced lattice thermal conductivity. Because total conductivity is the sum of lattice and electronic contributions, reducing the lattice term cannot by itself increase the total; no compensating increase in the electronic term is specified.

The hypothesis broadly says thermal conductivity will be improved, while the predicted outcome simultaneously specifies reduced lattice thermal conductivity without clearly stating which transport component is intended to improve.
